opportunities.title: Extractives super-cycle: copper, gold, and lithium capital reopening across the Andes
opportunities.narrative: The Andean region's defining opportunity in 2026 is a synchronized reopening of extractives capital across four of its five economies, each at a different stage of the same cycle. Peru's mining-linked investment is accelerating hard, with $2.05 billion committed in just the first four months of 2026 (up 43.5% y/y) and a projected $6.3 billion full-year total led by Southern Peru Copper Corporation (IndexBox, June 2026), underwritten by a current account surplus near 3.6% of GDP and government debt of just 30% of GDP (IMF). Ecuador's IMF-mandated reopening of its mining cadastre, targeted for end-June 2026, is set to unlock six copper and gold projects worth roughly $11 billion (Rio Times), even as the country posts a current account surplus of 5.9% of GDP. Bolivia is earlier in the cycle but moving in the same direction, with new mining and lithium rules expected in 2026 to restructure the tax and area-allocation regime for private capital (BNamericas, May 2026) -- 'contracted but contested,' not yet bankable at scale, but a genuine policy opening in a country otherwise contracting (-3.3% GDP growth, IMF 2026). Venezuela's Orinoco Belt heavy-crude assets, meanwhile, are attracting renewed major-IOC capital as sanctions ease -- Chevron's Petroindependencia expansion targets roughly 50% output growth from a 260,000 bpd base, and Shell is pursuing a new production deal (FDD, OFAC general licenses, June 2026). The common thread: regional resource wealth is being repriced upward by both energy-transition demand and reopening sanctions/regulatory regimes, with Peru offering the most bankable near-term exposure and Ecuador and Venezuela offering higher-beta entry points layered on visible security and political risk.

opportunities.title: Colombia's PPP infrastructure pipeline: financing continuity through political transition
opportunities.narrative: Colombia offers the region's clearest evidence that development-finance relationships can keep moving even as domestic politics turns volatile. Despite a razor-thin, historically contested presidential transition to Abelardo de la Espriella, fiscal slippage (public debt above 61% of GDP and a 6.2%-of-GDP deficit), and a five-year low in FDI, World Bank PPI data records over $3.8 billion in active greenfield and brownfield road and port projects moving forward largely undisturbed -- including the Puerto Salgar-Barrancabermeja-Curumani corridor ($1.14B), Buenaventura-Loboguerrero-Buga ($889M), and Troncal Magdalena 2 ($866M), all dated 2024. A parallel, repeatable utility-scale solar template -- spanning the Shangri-La, Sabanalarga, Caldas, La Dorada, and Erco Energia portfolios across 2023-2024 -- signals a maturing renewable-energy financing market with multiple sponsors willing to underwrite similar structures. This is a case where the PPP and multilateral pipeline (World Bank, DFC, and Chinese state lenders) is effectively decoupled from the near-term political and fiscal repricing risk, offering financing continuity even as headline macro and political indicators deteriorate.

opportunities.title: Peru and Ecuador power-and-logistics buildout: bankable mid-cycle infrastructure
opportunities.narrative: Beneath the extractives headlines, Peru and Ecuador both show sustained, lower-volatility infrastructure financing tracks that reward patient capital. In Peru, World Bank PPI data records continuous greenfield activity in transmission lines, substations, and utility-scale solar -- Matarani (97MW), San Martín, Sunny Solar, and Hanaqpampa -- across 2022-2024, spanning Lima, Ica, Ayacucho, and northern corridors, and signaling durable grid-expansion demand independent of the mining cycle. Ecuador's own PPI-tracked portfolio shows a comparable track record in power and seaport logistics, anchored by the $181 million Villonaco III wind plant and the $150 million Puerto Bolívar port expansion, both active as of 2023. With Peru's inflation contained near 1.5-2.5% (IMF/World Bank) and Ecuador running a current account surplus of 5.9% of GDP alongside near-full employment (3.3% unemployment, World Bank 2025), both countries offer macro conditions supportive of long-duration infrastructure finance -- provided investors underwrite Ecuador's security backdrop and Peru's post-transition political settlement separately from the underlying project economics.

Andean Region.regional_narrative:
The Andean region in mid-2026 is defined by an unusually sharp bifurcation between macro-fiscal soundness and acute political-security stress, with the two rarely aligning in the same country. Peru and Ecuador anchor the constructive end of the spectrum -- Peru with government debt at just 30% of GDP and a current account surplus near 3.6% of GDP (IMF/World Bank), Ecuador with a current account surplus of 5.9% of GDP, inflation near zero (0.7-2.9%), and IMF program compliance confirmed in an April 2026 Fifth Review. Colombia sits in the middle, with growth holding at 2.3-2.6% but fiscal slippage visible in a debt load above 60% of GDP and a widening deficit. Bolivia and Venezuela occupy the distressed end: Bolivia's debt is projected to climb to 102.7% of GDP with inflation near 20-21% and GDP contracting 3.3% in 2026, while Venezuela's government debt sits at an extraordinary 308.7% of GDP with inflation forecast at 387.4% (IMF, 2026) -- even as the same country posts the region's fastest projected real growth (4.0%, IMF 2026) on the back of oil-sector reopening.

This divergence is not simply a growth story -- it is a story of institutions and security running out of step with balance sheets. Peru's sound fundamentals coexist with a genuinely contested July 2026 presidential transition now before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights; Colombia's infrastructure pipeline continues to move even as its own presidential transition is "razor-thin" and historically contested; Ecuador's strong external accounts sit against Latin America's highest homicide rate and a mining regulator that was bombed the same month its cadastre reopened; Bolivia's lithium and mining reforms emerge directly out of a state of emergency that left at least 17 dead; and Venezuela's oil re-engagement with Chevron, Shell, and new buyers like India is unfolding in the immediate aftermath of a catastrophic earthquake that killed more than 3,000. Across all five countries, the region's capital-flow story is one of continued multilateral and IOC engagement -- World Bank PPI project pipelines, IMF program reviews, OFAC license easing -- proceeding on a track that is only loosely coupled to each country's domestic political volatility.

For a portfolio principal, the practical implication is that country selection within the Andes should weight institutional and security trajectories as heavily as headline macro prints. Peru and Colombia offer the most bankable near-term financing structures (mining capital formation and PPP-style infrastructure, respectively) precisely because their capital pipelines have already demonstrated resilience through political noise. Ecuador and Venezuela offer higher-beta, resource-driven upside that requires separate underwriting of security and disaster-recovery risk. Bolivia remains the outlier -- a reform narrative not yet matched by fiscal stabilization or bankable project scale.
Andean Region.risk_outlook: The region's principal risk is that political and institutional stress, not macro fundamentals, becomes the binding constraint on capital deployment. Peru's presidential transition remains formally contested through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, with a newly reconstituted Senate poised to determine whether the country's pattern of nine presidents in ten years repeats; Colombia's own transition to Abelardo de la Espriella is "historically contested" and coincides with a five-year low in FDI and a 6.2%-of-GDP deficit; Ecuador's security deterioration -- roughly 9,216 murders in 2025 and a bombed mining regulator -- sits directly astride its most promising extractives opportunity; Bolivia's state of emergency and at least 17 deaths from fuel-subsidy protests reflect social conflict that could resurface as further subsidy and mining-code reforms proceed against a backdrop of 102.7%-of-GDP debt and 20%-plus inflation; and Venezuela's fiscal position (308.7% debt-to-GDP, inflation forecast at 387.4%) is now further stressed by earthquake reconstruction costs even as its oil sector reopens to Western capital. None of these risks is hypothetical or boilerplate -- each is an active, dated event from the past several months -- and the correlated pattern across the region (contested elections, security shocks, and fiscal stress arriving in the same window as capital-market reopening) argues for treating political and security due diligence as a distinct, non-negotiable layer of any Andean investment thesis, separate from the macro screen.

opportunities.title: DRC's macro-security divergence as the region's highest-beta opportunity
opportunities.narrative: The Democratic Republic of Congo is the region's central paradox and its single largest opportunity set: IMF figures show real GDP growth accelerating to 5.9% in 2026 with inflation cooling to 3.3% and government debt among the lowest in the region at 24.6% of GDP, even as FDI inflows run at 3.8% of GDP -- among the strongest in Central Africa. That macro improvement is compounding with a global copper cycle in which prices have surged 36.8% over twelve months, feeding directly into DRC project financing momentum and reinforcing the firm's thesis that central-African copper producers are positioned to outperform over the coming year. The bankable evidence is already visible in the World Bank's PPI pipeline: the $1.2 billion Port of Banana seaport concession, the $208 million Eastcastle telecom tower build, and a cluster of off-grid solar hybrid mini-grid projects (Bunia/Goma/Kindu, Nuru, Essor -- collectively over $185 million since 2021) show repeat private-sector structuring even against a difficult security backdrop. The opportunity is real but geographically bounded -- it is a national-level growth and financing story that must be underwritten separately from the eastern conflict zone.

opportunities.title: Republic of Congo and Equatorial Guinea offshore hydrocarbons re-rating
opportunities.narrative: Offshore oil remains Central Africa's most consistently bankable asset class, and 2026 has brought fresh catalysts in both of the region's Gulf of Guinea producers. In the Republic of Congo, TotalEnergies' April 14, 2026 discovery at the Moho license adds an estimated 100 million recoverable barrels to an already-producing ~90,000 boe/d asset, a tie-back opportunity onto existing floating production infrastructure that arrives alongside renewed sovereign debt-market access -- $1.63 billion in Eurobond issuance between November 2025 and February 2026 despite gross debt near 91-97% of GDP. In Equatorial Guinea, the EG Ronda 2026 licensing round (24 blocks, open April-November) and Eni's six-block reconnaissance agreement show international upstream appetite persisting even as the broader economy contracts (-2.7% projected 2026 real GDP growth, IMF), suggesting investors are underwriting specific hydrocarbon assets independently of the sovereign's deteriorating macro and governance picture.

opportunities.title: Gabon's power, water and blue-finance pipeline amid fiscal retrenchment
opportunities.narrative: Gabon illustrates a region-wide pivot from China-financed, investment-heavy growth toward a more constrained, diversified-investor posture, and this repositioning is generating its own opportunity set. Even as the transitional government deprogrammed roughly CFAF 968.1 billion in public investment projects in May 2026 for lacking feasibility studies and gross debt climbs from 78.9% to 86.1% of GDP between 2025 and 2026 (IMF), FDI inflows remain the strongest in the region at 5.5% of GDP (World Bank, 2024), and a functioning PPI pipeline persists in power and water: Kinguélé Aval hydropower ($211.0 million), Ayème Plaine solar PV ($152.4 million), and Ntoum water treatment ($183.2 million), all active since 2021-2022. Beyond conventional infrastructure, the DFC's $747.8 million political risk insurance backing for Gabon's Blue Bonds for Marine Conservation signals that conservation-linked structured finance, guaranteed by US development finance instruments, is emerging as a genuine complementary channel to traditional project debt.

opportunities.title: CAR's post-transition normalization as an early-stage mining and multilateral re-entry play
opportunities.narrative: Central African Republic offers the region's most speculative but potentially highest-torque re-rating story: a UN-verified political normalization completed in mid-2026 (Touadéra's March 30 inauguration, National Assembly seated May 4, government formed May 21) coincides with IMF-projected disinflation to 1.5% in 2026, a narrowing current account deficit to -3.4% of GDP, and continued growth of 2.6%, together signaling a stabilizing macro-fiscal base that could support financing beyond the current Chinese-grant-dominated structure. The clearest precedent for large-ticket commercial capital remains the Bank of China's $200 million bonded-debt facility for CAR's mining sector (2021), positioning extractives as the most credible entry point for the next wave of institutional financing, provided investors ring-fence exposure away from the still-active northeast and southeast conflict zones in Vakaga, Haut-Mbomou, and Mbomou.

Central Africa.regional_narrative:
Central Africa in mid-2026 is a region of sharply diverging macro trajectories layered onto a remarkably consistent security and governance risk map. The commodity-linked economies -- DRC, Republic of Congo, and to a lesser extent Cameroon -- are seeing growth accelerate or hold steady (DRC's IMF-projected 5.9% in 2026 stands out as the region's fastest, against Cameroon's more modest 3.3% and Congo's 2.8%), while the region's other hydrocarbon producer, Equatorial Guinea, is contracting for a third consecutive year (-2.7% projected 2026 real GDP growth, IMF), an outlier that is now visibly destabilizing its own elite politics. FDI inflows tell a similarly bifurcated story: Gabon (5.5% of GDP) and DRC and Congo (3.8% each) are pulling in capital well above the regional norm, while CAR, Cameroon, and Equatorial Guinea cluster closer to 1.4-1.7% of GDP, reflecting a market that continues to reward resource-rich, infrastructure-financeable states over fragile or contracting ones.

The region's debt profile is the second defining axis of differentiation. DRC (24.6% of GDP) and Cameroon (39.3%) retain meaningful fiscal headroom under IMF 2026 projections, whereas Gabon (86.1%) and Republic of Congo (91.3%) are managing debt loads that leave, in the words of the firm's own Congo assessment, "little room for policy error" -- yet both have still found investor appetite, whether through Congo's $1.63 billion in recent Eurobond issuance or Gabon's DFC-guaranteed blue-bond structure. CAR's 64.0% debt-to-GDP sits in between, newly buttressed by a genuine political normalization that the World Bank/IMF numbers alone do not capture.

The unifying regional theme for 2026 is that national-level macro indicators are increasingly decoupled from subnational and elite-level political risk. DRC's improving macro picture coexists with an escalating eastern conflict and Ebola outbreak; Cameroon's stabilizing inflation and debt trajectory sit against an active Anglophone insurgency and an unresolved presidential succession; CAR's UN-verified institutional progress does not extend to its northeast and southeast prefectures; and Equatorial Guinea's economic contraction is now fusing with an intra-family resource-control contest at the top of government. For a portfolio principal, the region rewards granular, subnational risk-mapping far more than country-level aggregates.
Central Africa.risk_outlook: The region's principal risk is that structured-conflict indicators are lagging the reality on the ground across nearly every jurisdiction with a positive macro story. DRC's 5.9% growth and improving current account sit alongside an unresolved Rwanda relationship now escalated to an ICJ filing and an Ebola death toll surpassing 500 by early July 2026; Cameroon's disinflation and debt reduction coexist with a dispersed Anglophone insurgency, active Boko Haram/ISWAP incidents in the Far North, and an opaque presidential succession crisis centered on Biya's unexplained absence and an unfilled vice-presidency; and CAR's genuine post-transition normalization does not reach Vakaga, Haut-Mbomou, or Mbomou, where armed-group attacks and targeted killings continued into late June 2026. Layered on top is a fiscal-fragility risk cluster -- Gabon and Republic of Congo carrying debt above 85% of GDP even as they deprogram investment projects or lean on Eurobond refinancing, and Equatorial Guinea's outright economic contraction now visibly destabilizing the ruling family's internal cohesion. Collectively, these dynamics mean the region's headline growth and inflation improvements should be read as necessary but not sufficient signals; the binding constraint on capital deployment across Central Africa in 2026 is subnational security exposure and elite political fragility that official macro series do not price in.

opportunities.title: Nearshoring and services FDI along the Northern Triangle-Costa Rica-Panama corridor
opportunities.narrative: The region's strongest structural story is its emergence as a nearshoring and services-export platform for U.S.-facing supply chains, anchored by Costa Rica, Guatemala, and El Salvador. Costa Rica is growing at 4.6% in 2025 (World Bank) with FDI inflows at 5.6% of GDP (2024, World Bank), backed by a February 2026 Silicon Valley investment promotion office, a planned Singapore office, and a reported $830 million-plus project pipeline including medical-device manufacturer Insulet (Euronews, March 2026). Guatemala offers the cleanest balance-sheet complement to this story -- 3.9% IMF-projected 2026 growth, inflation at just 2.6%, and government debt of only 27.6% of GDP (IMF, 2026) -- while El Salvador, despite an 84.5%-of-GDP debt load, is delivering 3.3% growth with unemployment near historic lows (IMF, 2026) and an active DFC correspondent-banking channel through Banco Azul and Federación de Cajas de Crédito. Together these three economies show the region can offer investors a genuine growth-with-low-inflation combination increasingly scarce elsewhere in the hemisphere.

opportunities.title: Renewable-energy generation as the region's most bankable infrastructure template
opportunities.narrative: Across at least five countries -- Honduras, Guatemala, Nicaragua, the Dominican Republic, and Jamaica -- World Bank PPI data reveal a decade-plus, repeatable track record of financing utility-scale solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal projects that has survived multiple political cycles and, in Nicaragua's case, outright sanctions regimes. Honduras alone has hosted PPI-tracked renewable projects ranging from $69.3 million to $370 million between 2015 and 2023; Guatemala's pipeline spans Escuintla Biomass (2014) through the $64.0 million Yolanda Solar plant (2024); Nicaragua's legacy portfolio includes the $370 million Polaris Geothermal project and continues, diminished, with $12.5 million solar phases in 2023-2024; and the Dominican Republic has added a wave of new solar capacity (Mirasol/Peravia, Sajoma, Cotoperí, Montecristi) across 2022-2024. Jamaica's parallel utility-upgrade financing -- the $100 million JPS grid modernization and $77 million Rio Cobre water plant -- extends the same bankable-infrastructure logic to grid resilience. This is a rare case where the underlying project-finance structure has proven durable even where sovereign political risk (Nicaragua) or fiscal stress (Jamaica) would otherwise give investors pause.

opportunities.title: Dominican Republic tourism and record FDI as a regional growth anchor
opportunities.narrative: The Dominican Republic stands out as the region's clearest unambiguous growth story, posting a fourth consecutive record year of FDI at $5.03 billion in 2025 and a record-breaking first half of 2026 tourism season with 6.6 million arrivals (Tourism Minister David Collado, July 5, 2026), against IMF-projected 2026 real GDP growth of 3.7-4.5% and a government debt ratio easing to 58.3% of GDP. Costa Rica's tourism sector is running a parallel trajectory, with eight consecutive months of arrivals growth and a 9.4% year-over-year rise in air tourists through May 2026 (ICT data via The Costa Rica News). Together these two economies demonstrate that Caribbean and Central American tourism-and-FDI engines remain intact and expanding even as neighboring Jamaica absorbs a hurricane-driven contraction, underscoring that the region's tourism dividend is uneven but, where present, deep and repeatable.

opportunities.title: Panama's logistics and maritime corridor re-rating
opportunities.narrative: Panama's return to the Paris MOU maritime 'white list' (Hellenic Shipping News, July 2, 2026) via strengthened flag-state governance, combined with new MINSEG security funding and Colón Free Zone scanner deployments, signals a re-rating opportunity in shipping-registry, logistics-security, and counter-trafficking infrastructure tied to the Canal-adjacent corridor. This sits alongside continued headline growth of 3.8% (IMF, 2026) and 4.8% in Q1 per APEDE, though investors should weigh this opportunity against a 63.1% collapse in FDI in 2025 -- a divergence that reframes how much of Panama's growth is capital-deployment-driven versus reflecting unresolved Cobre Panamá concession and Canal-adjacent port-control tensions between the U.S. and China.

Central America & Caribbean.regional_narrative:
Central America and the Caribbean in mid-2026 present a region cleanly split between an orthodox-growth core and a cluster of acute fragility cases, with the median country -- Honduras, Nicaragua, the Dominican Republic, Guatemala, Panama -- delivering IMF-projected 2026 real GDP growth in the 3.3-3.9% band alongside inflation mostly contained in the low single digits. Guatemala's 27.6%-of-GDP debt load and Nicaragua's 4.2%-of-GDP current account surplus (2024, World Bank) sit at one end of a fiscal-space spectrum that runs through El Salvador's 84.5%-of-GDP debt and Jamaica's 65.8%-of-GDP debt at the other, meaning the region's growth convergence masks sharply divergent capacity to absorb shocks. The prevailing capital-flows story is nearshoring and services-FDI concentration in Costa Rica, Guatemala, and El Salvador, set against a Dominican Republic that is independently compounding a tourism-and-FDI boom (a fourth consecutive record FDI year at $5.03 billion in 2025) -- together these four economies plus Panama's logistics corridor represent the bulk of investable regional growth.

Set against this, three countries -- Haiti, Cuba, and to a lesser extent Nicaragua -- illustrate how macro stability and state capacity can decouple entirely. Haiti's economy is contracting for a seventh consecutive year (-1.7% in 2026, IMF) with inflation above 23% and roughly 2,300 gang-related deaths and 1.5 million displaced in 2026 alone (UN/IOM), a security collapse that dwarfs any macro signal. Cuba's near-term story is an energy-and-financing crisis -- a third nationwide blackout in six months, a reported Visa/Mastercard cutoff, and an IMF/EIU-projected 7.2% GDP contraction in 2026 following 3.8% contraction in 2025 -- driven by external sanctions pressure rather than domestic unrest. Nicaragua meanwhile shows the region's sharpest disconnect between headline macro (4.9% 2025 growth, low inflation, current account surplus) and institutional trajectory: FDI/GDP has been declining since 2022, the country turned net payer to multilateral creditors in 2024, and Western development-finance engagement has gone unrefreshed since FY2018 even as targeted international sanctions remain in force.

A third dynamic worth flagging for portfolio construction is that several countries' conflict and instability signals are partly artifacts of data contamination rather than genuine deterioration -- Panama's conflict-event count is substantially inflated by GDELT misattributions to unrelated U.S. Florida news, and the Dominican Republic's elevated headline conflict tagging is similarly thin once inspected. This means the region's true security-risk gradient is steeper and more binary than aggregate indices suggest: most countries (Costa Rica, Guatemala, Dominican Republic, Panama, El Salvador) sit in a genuinely low-conflict-intensity band, while Haiti sits in a category of its own and Honduras and Jamaica occupy an intermediate zone where political legitimacy questions (Honduras) or exogenous shocks (Jamaica's Hurricane Melissa-driven Q1 2026 output decline of 4.1% year-on-year) complicate otherwise stabilizing macro pictures.
Central America & Caribbean.risk_outlook: The region's principal risks are institutional and political rather than macroeconomic in the growth-core countries, and existential in the fragility cluster. In Honduras, a contested November 2025 election, a 31% approval rating for President Asfura after 100 days, a fragmented Congress, and the unresolved Próspera ISDS claim (still seeking $1.6 billion) mean political and legal risk sits closer to the surface than the IMF's stabilizing 3.3% growth and 43.8%-of-GDP debt figures suggest. Costa Rica's July 2026 executive-judiciary confrontation -- President Fernández's organized-crime-infiltration accusation against the courts and the Supreme Court's categorical rejection -- signals real institutional stress worth monitoring even absent street-level unrest. Guatemala's anti-corruption reform under new Attorney General García Luna is actively contested and could spill into regulatory unpredictability, while Panama's Cobre Panamá concession and Canal-adjacent U.S.-China port friction remain unresolved flashpoints layered atop a 63.1% FDI collapse. At the acute end, Haiti's security collapse (2,300 gang-related deaths, 1.5 million displaced in 2026) combined with the transitional council's July 7 ouster of the prime minister weeks before scheduled August 30 elections represents the region's most binding constraint on any investment thesis, while Cuba's compounding energy and external-financing crisis and Nicaragua's deepening diplomatic isolation under continued targeted sanctions mean both economies remain effectively closed to conventional Western capital regardless of headline growth data.

opportunities.title: East African power-generation and grid build-out
opportunities.narrative: Across the East African corridor, renewable and hydro-power generation is the single most consistently bankable theme in the World Bank's PPI dataset, spanning geothermal, wind, solar, and hydro assets from Djibouti to Rwanda and cutting across both fast-growers and post-conflict states. Ethiopia's newly completed 5.15-GW Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and the $271M Tulu Moye Geothermal Phase I sit alongside Kenya's ATIDI-mobilized $960M package for Lake Turkana Wind, Kipeto Wind and Menengai Geothermal (The Star, July 2026), Uganda's Achwa I hydro ($95M) and Ituka solar PV ($19M), Rwanda's Rukarara VI hydropower and AXIAN renewable portfolio, Burundi's Weza Power and Songa Energy projects, and Djibouti's operational Ghoubet Wind Farm ($123.5M) and Grand Bara solar plant. The breadth of financiers -- ATIDI, DFC, World Bank PPI-tracked greenfields, and bilateral technical assistance (DFC's $3.1M Virunga Power grant in Burundi) -- signals a multi-country, multi-financier pipeline that is largely decoupled from any single country's political cycle, even as growth rates supporting power demand range from Ethiopia's 9.2% and Rwanda's 7.2% (IMF, 2026) down to Kenya's steadier 4.5%.

opportunities.title: Regional ICT and digital-infrastructure buildout
opportunities.narrative: A second cross-cutting theme is the near-simultaneous expansion of broadband and data-center infrastructure across Djibouti, Tanzania, Rwanda, Uganda and Ethiopia, largely via the same private operators -- SEACOM and Raxio -- suggesting a regional connectivity thesis rather than a series of isolated national projects. SEACOM's broadband cable expansion appears at a near-identical $29.6M ticket size in Djibouti, Tanzania, and Rwanda (all World Bank PPI, 2023), while Raxio's colocation data-center portfolio recurs in Uganda and Ethiopia ($24.3M, 2023), and Ethiopia's telecom liberalization has drawn Safaricom's $257.4M 4G/5G expansion outside the state-to-state channel entirely. This is consistent with East Africa's positioning as a regional data-transit hub anchored by Djibouti's Red Sea cable landing points, and it gives investors exposure to digital infrastructure that is less correlated with the individual political risk running through Ethiopia, Uganda or Tanzania.

East Africa / Horn.regional_narrative:
East Africa and the Horn present the sharpest growth-versus-fragility divergence of any region the firm covers, with the same set of countries posting some of the world's strongest GDP prints even as several sit atop active insurgencies, contested elections, or open civil war. Ethiopia (9.2%), Rwanda (7.2%), Uganda (7.5%) and Djibouti (6.0%) all show IMF 2026 growth projections well above global averages, and Burundi's disinflation from 45% to 8.6% over twelve months (IMF Article IV, June 2026) is a genuine stabilization success story. Yet this same list includes Sudan, where 2026 inflation runs near 75%, government debt exceeds 169% of GDP, and unemployment sits above 61% against a backdrop of drone strikes and mass-atrocity findings in Kordofan and Darfur, and South Sudan, where a formally advancing peace process and a locked-in December 2026 election date coexist with 767 UNMISS-documented civilian deaths in three months. The region's investable core -- Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Ethiopia, Rwanda -- is financing itself through a genuinely diversified mix of Chinese state capital, DFC direct lending, World Bank PPI-tracked greenfield power and telecom projects, and multilateral vehicles like ATIDI, even as political risk is rising in several of the same markets in ways the macro data does not yet capture.

The defining regional dynamic is that capital continues to flow at scale precisely where security and political risk are most visibly deteriorating. Ethiopia's fifth ECF review completion and 5.15-GW dam commissioning sit alongside a Tigray-adjacent election that excluded major opposition regions; Uganda's 10.2%-projected growth on first oil revenue from EACOP sits alongside the abduction of an opposition lawyer and a UN statement on unresolved political detentions; Tanzania's 5.9% growth and falling 48.7%-of-GDP debt load sit alongside a reimposed rally ban ahead of July 2026 protests. This is not a region where opportunity and risk are sequential -- they are running in parallel across nearly every major economy, which argues for position-level rather than country-level risk management.

Financially, the region also shows a distinctive commodity and capital-flow linkage that sets it apart from a simple growth-story reading. South Sudan's conflict intensity tracks global copper, silver, gold, platinum and aluminum prices at zero lag (r ~0.5-0.7), consistent with a shared global liquidity or commodity super-cycle rather than local supply dynamics, while Kenya's unrest indicators lead renewed investment activity by three months -- both findings suggest that East African risk and East African opportunity are, in part, functions of global capital and commodity cycles rather than purely domestic political variables.
East Africa / Horn.risk_outlook: The region's downside risks cluster around three distinct but potentially compounding channels. First, active state fragmentation and war -- Sudan's Kordofan-centered conflict (45+ civilians killed by drone strikes in three weeks, UN News) and Darfur atrocity findings (Amnesty International, RSF crimes against humanity at El Fasher), alongside South Sudan's 767 civilian deaths in three months and SPLM-IO's explicit threat to treat voter registration as an act of war -- represent open-ended humanitarian and financing freezes with no near-term resolution. Second, a slower-burn authoritarian-consolidation risk is visible in Ethiopia (a landslide election excluding contested regions, CSIS assessing a worsening structural security outlook), Uganda (documented abductions and forced deportations of opposition-linked lawyers, UN Secretary-General statement on unresolved detentions) and Tanzania (a reimposed rally ban and pre-protest arrests), where strong headline growth is not yet pricing in rising political risk. Third, external and geopolitical spillover risk is concentrated in the Horn proper: Djibouti's port-and-transit economy sits directly astride an intensifying Red Sea shipping conflict, Eritrea faces a live possibility of renewed Ethiopia-Eritrea confrontation over Tigray, and Rwanda's otherwise strong fundamentals are bounded by US Treasury sanctions tied to its role in the eastern DRC conflict. Collectively, these risks argue for treating East Africa's growth numbers and its security trajectory as two independent data series that happen to be improving and deteriorating simultaneously, rather than assuming one will discipline the other.

Mexico.regional_narrative:
Mexico's economic story today is one of bifurcation rather than uniform slowdown. Headline growth has decelerated sharply -- from a robust labor market with unemployment near historic lows of 2.6-2.7% (World Bank, 2025) to GDP growth of just 0.6% in 2025 (World Bank), with the IMF projecting only a modest recovery to 1.6% real GDP growth in 2026. Inflation has stabilized in the high-3% range (3.8% World Bank 2025, 3.9% IMF 2026), and government debt sits at a manageable 62.7% of GDP (IMF, 2026), giving policymakers room to maneuver even as the current account remains marginally negative at -0.4% of GDP (World Bank, 2025).

The more consequential dynamic for capital allocators is sectoral divergence beneath these aggregate figures. Traditional nearshoring-driven manufacturing -- long the centerpiece of Mexico's post-pandemic investment thesis -- is showing concrete signs of reversal, most visibly in Toyota's decision to relocate Tacoma pickup production to a $3.6 billion Texas plant rather than expand Mexican capacity (CBS News, July 2026). Yet this has not translated into a broad capital flight: net FDI inflows remain solid at 2.5% of GDP (World Bank, 2024), redirected increasingly toward renewable energy, digital infrastructure, and fintech/SME lending rather than automotive assembly.

For a portfolio principal, the takeaway is that Mexico is no longer a single macro trade but a portfolio of sector-specific theses moving in different directions simultaneously. Energy generation and ICT/data-center infrastructure are absorbing large-ticket private financing and continue to look bankable on a standalone basis, while security deterioration and trade-integration risk since February 2026 are concentrating downside specifically in traditional export manufacturing and the broader nearshoring narrative that dominated market thinking through 2023-2024.
Mexico.risk_outlook: The principal risk to Mexico's outlook is not macroeconomic but structural and security-driven: the country assessment flags intensifying security conditions and deteriorating trade-integration dynamics since February 2026 as the key variables that could derail the broader investment case, independent of the still-stable inflation, debt, and unemployment readings. The Toyota relocation is the clearest market signal that nearshoring -- the thesis that anchored Mexican asset allocation for several years -- is beginning to reverse in at least one marquee sector, and a continuation of that pattern across autos and adjacent manufacturing would weigh on FDI composition even if the headline 2.5%-of-GDP inflow figure holds up. With GDP growth already soft at 0.6% in 2025 and only a modest IMF-projected recovery to 1.6% in 2026, Mexico has limited buffer to absorb a sustained manufacturing pullback without broader knock-on effects on employment and the current account, which is already in modest deficit.

Egypt adds scale and diversification risk-appetite: the Gulf of Suez wind, Abydos solar, Amunet wind and Green Hydrogen projects (World Bank PPI, 2022-2024) plus Scatec's flagged $5 billion multi-year renewables/desalination/data-center program point to state-backed capacity additions running parallel to the IMF-anchored stabilization program. The common thread — completed-and-active greenfield structures with repeat sponsors (Scatec, Qair) across three different sovereign risk profiles — makes this the region's clearest sector-level, cross-border opportunity rather than a single-country story.

North Africa.regional_narrative:
North Africa in mid-2026 presents a region split cleanly into two macro tiers, with the divide running less along conflict exposure than along fiscal and reform credibility. Morocco and Algeria anchor the stable tier: Morocco posts 4.9% projected 2026 growth (IMF) with inflation near 1.3% and a gently declining debt ratio (67.1% to 65.8% of GDP), while Algeria holds growth near 3.8-3.9% with inflation easing sharply and its current account deficit narrowing to just -1.0% of GDP. Egypt occupies a more leveraged position — growth of 4.2-5% and a genuine disinflation trajectory (from 20.4% down to a projected 13.2%, IMF) are being rewarded by markets (a 20.7% year-to-date EGX30 rally) and underwritten by extraordinary FDI inflows of 12.0% of GDP, but government debt at 87.0% of GDP is the highest in the region and inflation, while falling, remains in double digits. Tunisia and Libya sit at the fragile end: Tunisia's 84.9%-of-GDP debt load and stalled IMF program are forcing recourse to market borrowing and central-bank deficit financing, while Libya's 13.4% headline growth figure reflects a low, war-disrupted base rather than durable expansion.

The region's capital-flow story is increasingly bifurcated by sector rather than by country. A renewables-and-desalination financing template — pioneered at scale in Morocco (Noor Midelt CSP-PV at $837.5M) and Egypt (a Scatec-flagged $5 billion multi-year program) and replicated at smaller scale in Tunisia (Sidi Bouzid/Tozeur solar) — has become the closest thing to a pan-regional asset class, attracting repeat sponsors across sharply different sovereign risk profiles. Digital infrastructure tells a similar cross-border story: the $71.8 million MEDUSA submarine cable project threads through Algeria, Tunisia and Libya simultaneously, offering a rare diversification vehicle that is largely insulated from each country's idiosyncratic political risk. What is notably absent this cycle is a unifying regional shock or correlation signal — the cross-cutting evidence base is empty — which itself is informative: the five economies are currently being priced and reformed on distinctly national tracks rather than moving together.

Political legitimacy and fiscal sustainability, not conflict, are the swing factors an executive should track. Algeria's constructive macro numbers sit against a July parliamentary election that drew roughly 21% turnout after a third of candidates were disqualified — a widening gap between formal process and public engagement that the IMF's otherwise favorable Article IV assessment does not resolve. Tunisia's stalled IMF negotiations, with President Saied rejecting subsidy-cut conditionality, are pushing the sovereign toward a ~€2 billion 2026 market raise and parliament-authorized zero-interest central-bank financing — a fragile equilibrium that avoids default while building inflationary and institutional risk. Libya's political track (a June 18 tripartite roadmap toward February 2027 elections, first unified budget since 2013) is outrunning its security track, evident in the May 8 Zawiya refinery clashes. Egypt alone carries a genuine external-shock exposure, sitting adjacent to an intensifying Israel-Iran-Hezbollah conflict theater even as its own reform program strengthens.
North Africa.risk_outlook: The region's principal vulnerability is not a shared conflict shock but a set of parallel, country-specific fault lines that could each independently derail otherwise constructive macro trajectories. Egypt's stabilization dividend is the most acute case: a reform program earning a staff-level EFF agreement and a 20.7% equity rally sits directly next to an active and intensifying Israel-Iran-Hezbollah conflict theater, meaning any escalation carries direct spillover risk to Suez-corridor trade volumes and investor sentiment that cannot be hedged away from the reform story itself. Tunisia's financing approach — central-bank deficit monetization authorized up to 7 billion dinars at zero interest, layered on a stalled IMF program and 84.9%-of-GDP debt — is a classic fragile-equilibrium setup where near-term default avoidance is being purchased with inflation and central-bank-independence risk that analysts are already flagging. Algeria's widening gap between an improving macro picture and a historically low-turnout, heavily disqualified electoral process is a legitimacy risk that a debt-service trajectory the IMF itself calls a medium-term reserve concern could compound. Libya remains the most binary case: political and fiscal coordination (the tripartite roadmap, unified budget) is visibly outpacing security-sector unification, and the rejected Haftar-Dbeibeh power-sharing leak alongside the May Zawiya refinery clashes shows how quickly hydrocarbons-adjacent infrastructure bets could be disrupted before the February 2027 election window closes. Morocco is the outlier with no comparable overhang, though its export-diversification gains remain exposed to global demand for automotive and battery-materials output rather than to domestic instability.

Southern Africa.regional_narrative:
Southern Africa in mid-2026 is a region of genuinely divergent macro trajectories bound together by a common financing theme: renewable energy and resource-corridor capital continues to flow even where fiscal and political conditions are deteriorating. At one end, Zimbabwe is posting IMF-projected growth near 5.0% with inflation collapsing from 81.4% to a projected 8.0%, and Zambia has pushed inflation down to 6.5% by June 2026 -- the lowest since February 2018 -- while rebuilding reserves to 4.4 months of import cover and completing roughly 94% of its debt-restructuring perimeter. At the other end, Mozambique's current account is projected to widen to -43.0% of GDP with debt at 106.1% of GDP, Botswana has seen debt jump from 38.6% to 47.0% of GDP alongside an 8.9%-of-GDP fiscal deficit tied to the diamond downturn, and Malawi is contending with a current account deficit near -18.8% of GDP and inflation still above 24%. South Africa, the region's anchor economy, sits in between: sovereign credit upgrades from Moody's, S&P, and Fitch between May and June 2026 reflect a third consecutive primary fiscal surplus, even as growth remains stuck near 1.0-1.1% and unemployment above 32%.

The unifying capital-markets story is that renewable power generation has become the region's default bankable asset class, spanning nearly every country regardless of fiscal condition, while a parallel and much larger hydrocarbons and critical-minerals capex cycle is concentrating transformative capital in specific corridors -- Mozambique's LNG basin, Namibia's offshore Orange and Walvis basins, and Angola's Lobito rail-and-port corridor. This is capital rotating toward energy transition and supply-chain-diversification themes even in markets carrying real fiscal strain, a pattern consistent with global institutional appetite for African critical minerals and gas rather than a signal of underlying macro health.

The region's political-economy risk, however, is increasingly cross-border rather than contained within single states. Anti-migrant unrest in South Africa serious enough to prompt a 3,000-plus troop deployment has produced a genuine humanitarian and diplomatic crisis for Malawi, whose diaspora has suffered over 33,000 deportations since June 2026 -- a reminder that GDELT-style country risk scores can mask cross-border spillover that has little to do with a country's own domestic stability. Meanwhile succession politics in Zimbabwe (Constitutional Amendment Bill No. 3), governance contestation in Eswatini, and Botswana's commodity-driven fiscal shock illustrate that political risk in the region is now as often institutional and cross-border as it is conflict-driven.
Southern Africa.risk_outlook: The region's principal risks cluster around three distinct fault lines rather than a single narrative. First, social and political strain in South Africa -- driven by unemployment above 32% despite fiscal consolidation -- has already produced a nationwide security response and a documented humanitarian spillover into Malawi (over 33,000 deportations, at least three deaths in transit), a dynamic that could deepen regional diplomatic friction even as South African sovereign credit metrics improve. Second, unresolved political contestation sits atop otherwise-stabilizing macro pictures in Zimbabwe (the succession dispute triggered by Constitutional Amendment Bill No. 3 and an open break between Mnangagwa and Chiwenga) and Eswatini (corruption allegations tied to the monarchy's largest recent infrastructure deal), meaning governance risk could reassert itself even where inflation and growth trends look constructive. Third, fiscal fragility is building in commodity- and aid-dependent economies -- Botswana's diamond-driven deficit swing, Mozambique's 106.1%-of-GDP debt load alongside a chronic Cabo Delgado insurgency near its gas assets, and Zambia's narrowing primary surplus (falling from 3.1% to 1.1% of GDP in 2026) ahead of a closely-watched election -- any of which could unwind recent stabilization gains if post-crisis fiscal discipline lapses or a successor IMF program fails to materialize.

opportunities.title: Copper- and lithium-linked extractives financing across the Andean-Argentine belt
opportunities.narrative: Chile and Argentina anchor a region-wide extractives financing cycle that is increasingly de-risked by policy design and geology alike. In Argentina, the RIGI incentive regime has already approved thirteen projects worth more than $42B in committed investment, including a combined $2.1B green-lit on May 14, 2026 for the San Jorge copper project in Mendoza and the Cauchari-Olaroz lithium expansion in Jujuy -- evidence that the fiscal-consolidation story (government debt easing to 70.4% of GDP, inflation falling to 30.4% by 2026 per IMF) is being paired with a genuine large-ticket resource pipeline. Next door, Chile's IMF Article IV consultation (July 6, 2026) ties its projected growth rebound from 1.8% in 2026 to 2.6% in 2027 directly to higher copper prices, a thesis reinforced on the ground by Marimaca Copper's high-grade bornite intercepts at Pampa Medina (6m at 6.11% Cu). Together the two countries offer complementary exposure: Argentina's policy-driven greenfield approvals and Chile's exploration-stage upside within an established mining belt.

opportunities.title: Repeatable power-sector project finance in Brazil and Argentina
opportunities.narrative: The Southern Cone's two largest economies are demonstrating a mature, bankable renewables pipeline that persists independent of political noise. Brazil's World Bank PPI records show continued structuring at scale -- the 846MW Serra do Assuruá wind complex ($638.2M) and multiple solar complexes in the $80-240M range -- consistent with the IMF's June 1, 2026 Article IV characterization of the economy as "remarkably resilient" even as 2026 growth eases to 1.9% and debt climbs to 96.5% of GDP. Argentina's parallel track record -- wind and solar builds from General Levalle to the MSU Energy solar portfolio and Genneia expansion, with ticket sizes from $33M to $260M across 2022-2024 -- shows the greenfield/brownfield renewables market survived the country's disinflation crisis intact. Financing competition adds a further dimension in Brazil, where Chinese state financiers (China Development Bank, Bank of China, ICBC, China Eximbank) remain active alongside a smaller US DFC footprint around grid assets tied to State Grid Brazil Holding and Petrobras, signaling the country remains a contested destination for both financing blocs.

opportunities.title: Paraguay's toll-road and financial-intermediation PPP pipeline amid the region's fastest growth
opportunities.narrative: Paraguay stands out as the Southern Cone's macro outperformer and its most under-owned infrastructure story: 6.0-6.6% GDP growth in 2025 (the strongest in 12 years per President Peña's July 1, 2026 address), inflation moderating toward 3.3%, and government debt contained near 37.8% of GDP -- a fiscal profile far lighter than Argentina's or Brazil's. That stability underwrites a genuinely repeatable public-private structuring model: World Bank PPI records a sequence of toll-road concessions spanning nearly three decades, from Ruta No. 07 (1998) through the $738.0M Route 2/7 Expansion (2019) to the $135.0M Concepción-Vallemi-San Lázaro concession (2023). A parallel, equally durable channel runs through development finance into the banking sector, with DFC direct lending and guaranty facilities to Sudameris Bank, Banco Regional, and Financiera Finexpar across FY2018-FY2022 establishing precedent for exposure to Paraguayan SME credit markets.

opportunities.title: Uruguay's institutional infrastructure pipeline and regional hospitality capital
opportunities.narrative: Despite a governance scare at the presidential level, Uruguay's underlying capital-formation channels remain active and are being used by regional players as a stability play. World Bank PPI records a sustained sequence of toll-road and transmission concessions -- Circuito 5, Circuito 6, Circuito Vial 2/7, and the Salto Transmission Line, all 2021-2022 -- that reflect the institutional durability historically associated with Uruguay's 66.8%-of-GDP debt load and low, moderate inflation (4.0% in 2026, IMF). That same stability narrative is drawing cross-border capital into hospitality real estate: a $500 million Brazilian-led acquisition and upgrade of a Punta del Este hotel, reported in April 2026, signals continued regional appetite for Uruguayan tourism assets even as FDI net inflows read negative (-4.8% of GDP, 2024, World Bank) on a headline basis -- likely reflecting repatriation or divestiture noise rather than a break in the underlying investment thesis.

Southern Cone.regional_narrative:
The Southern Cone in mid-2026 is a region of two speeds and one shared vulnerability. Paraguay and Argentina are growing fastest -- 6.0-6.6% and 4.4% respectively in 2025 World Bank data, with IMF 2026 projections of 4.2% and 3.5% -- while Brazil, Chile, and Uruguay are settling into a slower, steadier 1.8-2.5% band. What unites all five is that macro stabilization is real and measurable almost everywhere -- Argentine inflation collapsing from 211% at end-2023 toward an IMF-projected 30.4% in 2026, Chilean and Uruguayan inflation both converging near 4%, Paraguayan debt contained near 38% of GDP -- yet every one of these stabilization stories is running in parallel with a political-credibility deficit: Milei's approval at 36% amid a corruption scandal, Chile's new president already at roughly 40% approval within a hundred days, and Uruguay's Orsi collapsing to 20% approval amid an ethics scandal that has since widened. The region's investment case, in other words, is a macro-political arbitrage: balance sheets are healing faster than governments are earning public trust.

Capital allocation patterns reflect this bifurcation. Brazil remains the largest and most contested financing destination, with Chinese state financiers (China Development Bank, Bank of China, ICBC, China Eximbank) sustaining engagement in grid and infrastructure assets alongside a smaller US DFC presence, even as government debt climbs to 96.5% of GDP -- the highest in the region -- and the IMF's June 2026 Article IV mission still calls the economy "remarkably resilient." Chile is drawing record foreign inflows into its peso bond market in 2026 as the central bank cuts rates, a signal that fixed-income investors are pricing relative macro stability into a cyclically soft patch (Q1 2026 GDP growth of just 0.2% y/y per OECD). Argentina, by contrast, is attracting sector-specific, policy-incentivized capital through RIGI-approved mining and established renewables project finance rather than broad-based portfolio inflows, consistent with FDI net inflows still modest at 1.8% of GDP.

The smaller economies -- Paraguay and Uruguay -- offer the cleanest balance-sheet stories in the region, with debt-to-GDP near 38% and 67% respectively against Brazil's 96.5% and Argentina's 70.4%, but neither is immune to the governance-credibility theme: Paraguay carries name-specific US Treasury sanctions risk even amid record growth, while Uruguay's twin ethics scandals have hit presidential approval harder than any macro shock has hit its debt or inflation profile. For a principal weighing regional exposure, the throughline is that quantitative stabilization -- in growth, inflation, and debt -- is outpacing political and institutional consolidation almost everywhere south of the Amazon.
Southern Cone.risk_outlook: The Southern Cone's principal risk in this window is not conflict or systemic financial distress -- the automated conflict feed shows no substantively real security signals, and Brazil's headline "violence" hits are confirmed GDELT actor-matching artifacts tied to unrelated stories -- but a cluster of governance and political-credibility shocks landing simultaneously across four of five countries. Argentina's Milei faces a corruption scandal that forced out his Cabinet chief and a 1.5% monthly activity contraction that complicates the IMF's 3.5% growth projection; Chile's new president has already burned through much of his political capital within a hundred days against a backdrop of near-stagnant Q1 growth; Uruguay's Orsi has seen approval collapse to 20% amid a widening ethics scandal; and Paraguay, while security-quiet and macro-strong, carries idiosyncratic US Treasury sanctions exposure tied to specific individuals. Brazil's genuine risk narrative -- the Banco Master fraud probe and organized-crime enforcement in its largest metros -- sits apart from political approval dynamics but adds a distinct governance-quality overhang onto an already-rising 96.5%-of-GDP debt trajectory. None of these are individually destabilizing to the regional growth or disinflation story, but their concurrence raises the risk that policy continuity -- particularly around Argentina's RIGI regime and Chile's copper-linked recovery thesis -- could face disruption if any single approval crisis metastasizes into snap elections, cabinet paralysis, or reform reversal.

opportunities.title: Power-sector greenfield financing as the region's most repeatable bankable template
opportunities.narrative: Across nearly every West African/Sahel country reviewed -- from Benin and Togo to Chad, Mali, Burkina Faso, Guinea, Côte d'Ivoire, Senegal and Sierra Leone -- the single most consistent thread in the financing record is solar and hybrid power generation structured through the World Bank's Private Participation in Infrastructure (PPI) mechanism. This is a genuinely regional phenomenon: Côte d'Ivoire's Kong (50MW, $60.7M), Bondoukou ($60.0M) and Singrobo-Ahouaty hydropower ($183.7M) deals sit alongside Senegal's Niakhar, Walo and Kolda solar-plus-storage cluster and the Saint Louis CCGT ($475M), Guinea's 180MW Kankan-Siguiri-Kouroussa-Boké-Linsan solar PV project tied explicitly to Simandou 2040, and even conflict-affected Mali (Touna $128M, Fana $56M) and Chad (Djermaya Solar $41.4M) continuing to attract greenfield capital through active insurgencies. The pattern suggests power-generation project finance has become the region's most durable capital channel, largely insulated from the political volatility affecting other sectors, and is increasingly being financed on a repeatable structure regardless of a given country's governance trajectory.

opportunities.title: Guinea-Simandou iron-ore corridor and gold-mining state-partnership extractives
opportunities.narrative: Guinea stands out with an 8.7% IMF-projected 2026 growth rate -- among the strongest in the region -- driven substantially by bauxite output and the Simandou iron-ore program, a trajectory reinforced by continued private capital in mining-adjacent power and telecom (Orange Guinea's $227.4M brownfield ICT portfolio, World Bank PPI, 2023) even as the state renegotiates mining contracts. This sits alongside a broader gold and extractives theme spanning Mali and Burkina Faso, where sovereign mining vehicles (Burkina Faso's Siniyan-Sigui fund, the state's move to a 40% stake in Kiaka gold mine) are being stood up precisely as gold's 12-month rally of +26.4% keeps West African gold-mining equities bid; gold alone accounts for over 80% of Burkina Faso's export revenue. The opportunity set is concentrated in Guinea for iron-ore-linked infrastructure over an 18-month horizon and in Mali/Burkina Faso for gold-extractives equities over 6-12 months, with the caveat that both are increasingly structured around state-partnership rather than open concession models.

opportunities.title: Ghana-Côte d'Ivoire cocoa financing and disinflation convergence
opportunities.narrative: Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire together anchor a coastal-economy convergence story: both show accelerating disinflation and current-account improvement even as global cocoa supply tightness drives a 61% three-month price spike, keeping cocoa-exposed agribusiness processors and soft-commodity futures elevated over a 6-month horizon. Ghana's IMF-projected inflation path from 14.2% (2025) toward 5.8% (2026) alongside a current account surplus near 10.1% of GDP is reinforced by a repeatable cocoa receivables financing template -- the COCOBOD syndicated facility with Bank of China and ICBC, running $53-54M annual tranches within a $1.3-1.5 billion facility across multiple crop seasons. Côte d'Ivoire complements this with a $209 billion National Development Plan through 2030 built on 70% private-capital participation (allAfrica, July 2026) and its own maturing PPI power and port pipeline, including the $468.3M Côte d'Ivoire Terminal deal, signaling that West Africa's two largest cocoa producers are simultaneously deepening trade-finance infrastructure and diversifying beyond commodity dependence.

opportunities.title: Frontier reform openings in Mauritania and Gambia
opportunities.narrative: Two smaller, lower-profile economies are quietly building genuine reform-driven investment cases. Mauritania's Investment Code 2025 has already yielded IFC-reported approval of 19 projects worth roughly $120 million and an estimated 939 direct jobs since July 2025, layered atop sustained FDI inflows of 13.2% of GDP tied to the Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas project (World Bank, 2024) and a fiscal picture where debt is falling from 40.1% to a projected 37.1% of GDP (IMF). The Gambia, meanwhile, is disinflating from 7.9% toward a projected 5.8% in 2026 with a December 2025 policy rate cut to 16% and its first primary fiscal surplus since 2019, alongside a tourism recovery (arrivals up from 224,472 to 233,113, World Bank) that supports hospitality and agro-processing plays. Both openings are real but narrow, and both sit against near-term political stress -- a December 2026 Gambian election cycle shadowed by a fractured opposition and a security-establishment corruption scandal -- that argues for treating the reform momentum as an early-stage rather than fully de-risked opportunity.

West Africa / Sahel.regional_narrative:
West Africa and the Sahel in mid-2026 present the starkest macro-security divergence of any region the firm covers: headline growth and disinflation figures across nearly every country in the bloc look genuinely constructive, while a parallel track of open-web and specialist reporting -- largely invisible in structured event data -- documents an accelerating security and governance deterioration concentrated in the Sahelian core. IMF projections show Guinea growing at 8.7%, Benin at 7.0%, Niger at 6.7%, and Côte d'Ivoire above 6% for 2026, with regional inflation broadly retreating (Ghana from 14.2% toward 5.8%, Gambia from 7.9% toward 5.8%, Chad collapsing toward 0.5%). Yet this is occurring alongside the fall of Kidal to Tuareg and JNIM forces in Mali, a coordinated ISSP assault that killed over 85 Nigerien soldiers in June, a JNIM strike on Niamey's international airport (the third airport-targeting incident in the Sahel in six months, per ACLED), Sudan-war spillover into Chad's border regions, and Burkina Faso's diplomatic rupture with France alongside the dissolution of 118 civil society organizations. The coastal states -- Ghana, Côte d'Ivoire, Senegal, Benin, Togo -- remain comparatively insulated but not immune, as JNIM's cross-border reach into northern Benin and Côte d'Ivoire illustrates.

The region's capital-flow story is bifurcating along a similar axis. Multilateral and World Bank PPI-tracked power-sector financing continues almost uninterrupted regardless of security conditions -- greenfield solar deals are being financed in Mali and Chad even as insurgencies intensify -- while Chinese state grants and concessional financing remain the dominant or sole channel in Mali, Burkina Faso, Sierra Leone, Liberia and Mauritania's legacy financing base, a durability that likely reflects Beijing's higher political-risk tolerance relative to Western development finance. Meanwhile, a distinct fiscal-stress cluster is emerging around debt sustainability: Senegal's debt-to-GDP has reached 132.3% against a widening current account deficit, Guinea-Bissau sits at 73.6%, Gambia at 68.3%, and Togo is climbing from 63.0% toward 64.7% -- even as Nigeria (32.3%) and Chad (29.9%) show the opposite trend, underscoring that debt trajectories are diverging sharply within the region rather than moving as a single bloc.

Nigeria, as the regional anchor economy, illustrates the fragility beneath the stabilization narrative: a current account surplus near 5.8% of GDP and debt easing to 32.3% coexist with inflation that re-accelerated to nearly 16% in mid-2026 on fuel-price pass-through from the March Middle East oil shock, and a security threat that has moved from civilian and school targeting to direct assaults on military installations. This pattern -- solid aggregate numbers vulnerable to a single external or security shock -- is arguably the defining regional risk for the year ahead.
West Africa / Sahel.risk_outlook: The region's principal risk is that jihadist and insurgent violence -- JNIM, ISSP, and allied Tuareg forces -- has moved decisively from rural insurgency to strikes on state capacity itself: the fall of Kidal and assassination of Mali's defence minister, the Niamey airport assault, and attacks on Nigerian and Chadian military installations all signal contested state control in the Sahelian interior that structured economic data is not yet pricing. This core-Sahel crisis is bleeding outward into coastal states through cross-border attacks on Beninese and northern Ivorian positions, meaning the "Sahel risk" can no longer be geographically ring-fenced from the coastal growth story. Layered on top are distinct governance and institutional risks -- Burkina Faso's rupture with France and civil-society crackdown, Senegal's constitutional referendum amid a Faye-Sonko rupture, Guinea-Bissau's flagged election uncertainty, and Gambia's pre-election fracturing alongside a security-establishment corruption scandal -- each of which could independently disrupt capital flows even absent direct violence. Finally, fiscal fragility in Senegal (132.3% debt-to-GDP), Guinea-Bissau, Gambia, and Togo, combined with Nigeria's demonstrated sensitivity to external energy-price shocks, means the region's disinflation and growth narrative remains conditional on both continued external financing access and the absence of further global commodity shocks.
